questions.question: What does the multiplication rule state for events $A$ and $B$ with $P(A)>0$?
Equating the two forms $P(A)P(B\mid A)=P(B)P(A\mid B)$ and solving for $P(A\mid B)$ gives:
In $P(A)P(B\mid A)$, what does $P(B\mid A)$ represent?
options: The chance of $A$ after knowing $B$ occurred
The chance of $B$ after knowing $A$ occurred

questions.question: When applying the chain rule $P(A\cap B\cap C)=P(A)P(B\mid A)P(C\mid A\cap B)$, the events may be taken in:
options: any order (it gives the same product)

questions.question: For independent events, what happens to the conditional factor in the multiplication rule?
options: It becomes zero for every event
It reduces to the marginal probability
It must be larger than one

questions.question: If $P(A)=0.5$ and $P(B\mid A)=0.2$, what is $P(A\cap B)$?
A customer clicks an ad with probability $0.1$ and buys with probability $0.3$ given click. What is the probability of click and buy?
Which situation naturally uses the multiplication rule?
options: Taking the complement of one event

questions.question: If $P(A)=0.8$ and $P(B\mid A)=0.5$, what is $P(A\cap B)$?
Passing a first test has probability $0.9$, and passing a second test given the first is $0.8$. What is the probability of passing both?
How does the multiplication rule extend to several events?
options: As a sum of all marginal probabilities, in all instances without exception.
As a product of complements only
As a product of successive conditional probabilities
As a count of unordered selections

questions.question: Why is the multiplication rule not the same as assuming independence?
options: It can only be used for disjoint events
The conditional factor may differ from the marginal probability
It applies only when probabilities are equal, universally and without exception.

questions.question: Which formula follows by swapping the order of the events when $P(B)>0$?
Two cards are drawn without replacement. What expression gives the probability both are aces?
If $P(A\cap B)=0.18$ and $P(A)=0.6$, what is $P(B\mid A)$?
If two independent events have $P(A)=0.4$ and $P(B)=0.5$, what is $P(A\cap B)$?
Why does the multiplication rule $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B\mid A)$ require $P(A)>0$?
options: because $A$ must be the whole sample space
because $P(B\mid A)=P(A\cap B)/P(A)$ is undefined when $P(A)=0$

questions.question: What mistake is made by writing $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$ without checking independence?
options: It replaces a conditional probability by a marginal probability without justification
It conditions on an impossible event
It uses a partition that is not exhaustive, irrespective of the particular case.

questions.question: A machine is overloaded with probability $0.2$. Given overload, failure probability is $0.15$. What is the probability of overload and failure?
If $P(A)=0.25$, $P(B\mid A)=0.8$, and $P(C\mid A\cap B)=0.5$, what is the product for $P(A\cap B\cap C)$?
